questions.prompt: Why is OIDC (workload identity federation) preferred over a service principal secret for pipeline authentication?

options.text: It uses a short-lived token with no stored secret to leak or rotate
It removes the need for any permissions in Azure
It only works for private repositories

questions.explanation: OIDC lets the pipeline prove its identity with a short-lived token and no stored secret — so there's nothing to leak or rotate, unlike a stored client secret.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CI/CD are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: CI automatically builds and tests every change
GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines are both YAML-based CI/CD tools
Environments can require a manual approval before deploying to production
Storing long-lived secrets in the repo is the recommended auth method

questions.explanation: CI builds/tests changes; Actions and Pipelines are YAML tools; environments support approvals. Prefer OIDC over storing long-lived secrets.
CI is Continuous Integration — automatically building and testing every change so problems surface immediately.

items.text: Log in to Azure with OIDC

questions.explanation: A typical workflow checks out code, authenticates to Azure (OIDC), builds and tests, then deploys.

pairs.right: Auto build and test on every change
